meta.title: Who really said "Making money is art and working is art and good business is the best art"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, Warhol wrote it — the last line of the "business art" passage in The Philosophy of Andy Warhol (1975), and it is almost always quoted without its setup.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Making money is art and working is art and good business is the best art'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Andy Warhol: The Philosophy of Andy Warhol (From A to B and Back Again), Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1975, p. 92 — usually quoted minus its setup.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is a real Warhol sentence, not a motivational-poster invention: it closes the “business art” passage in The Philosophy of Andy Warhol (From A to B and Back Again), published by Harcourt Brace Jovanovich in 1975, where Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ cites it at p. 92. The catch is that it is almost never quoted with the setup Warhol gave it.

source.heading: Where it comes from

source.excerpt: During the hippie era people put down the idea of business — they’d say ‘Money is bad’, and ‘Working is bad’, but making money is art and working is art and good business is the best art.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ files the full business-art passage in its sourced 1970s section under The Philosophy of Andy Warhol: (From A to B and Back Again), 1975, citing p. 92.

The surrounding sentences were already being quoted from the book in the year it appeared: Wikipedia’s reception section ↗ reproduces John Raymond’s review in The Atlanta Journal-Constitution of 31 August 1975, which quotes Warhol on going “into business art” and on being good in business being the most fascinating kind of art.
Catalog records agree on the imprint and the date: Open Library ↗ lists the 1975 Harcourt Brace Jovanovich first edition alongside the 1977 and 2006 reprints.
A scan of that first edition — 266 pages, Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1975 — is held at the Internet Archive ↗, where it is access-restricted and available only through controlled lending.
source.excerptNote: Warhol reaches this line at the end of a short run about leaving “the thing called art” for business art and wanting to be a business artist — the sentence quoted everywhere is the last beat of that argument, not a standalone aphorism.

author.name: Andy Warhol
author.heading: Who was Andy Warhol?
author.bio: Born Andrew Warhola in Pittsburgh to immigrant parents from what is now Slovakia, Warhol took a BFA in Pictorial Design from Carnegie Institute of Technology in 1949 and spent the 1950s as one of New York’s most successful commercial illustrators, with clients including Tiffany & Co., The New York Times, Columbia Records and NBC. He turned that commercial fluency into fine art in the early 1960s — the 1962 Campbell’s Soup Cans made him famous — and from 1963 built a practice on commissioned portraits, films and magazine publishing. The line about business being the best art is not a stray provocation; it is the thesis of a career that refused to treat commerce and art as opposites.

misattribution.heading: The attribution is right. The quoting is usually wrong.
misattribution.intro: Unusually for a famous-name quote, nothing here needs debunking on authorship — Warhol really did put these words in print. What goes wrong is everything around them.

items.why: In the book the sentence is a reply, not a slogan. Wikiquote’s sourced text ↗ shows it arriving after Warhol sets the scene: “During the hippie era people put down the idea of business — they’d say ‘Money is bad’, and ‘Working is bad’…” Quoted bare, the deadpan disappears and it reads as an earnest business maxim.

It circulates as a spoken one-liner, but the documented source is a book: The Philosophy of Andy Warhol (From A to B and Back Again) ↗, Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1975. No dated speech or interview is needed to support it — and none should be invented for it.

Wikipedia’s account of the book records that it was ghostwritten by Pat Hackett and Bob Colacello, largely from taped interviews Hackett did with Warhol and taped conversations involving Colacello and Brigid Berlin. The words are Warhol’s; the transcription and shaping were not.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuine, sourced, and routinely mangled: the line closes the business-art passage of Warhol’s 1975 book ↗. If you quote it, quote the hippie-era setup with it.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Warhol had spent the 1950s drawing shoes and record sleeves for hire before he was ever a gallery artist, and he never pretended the two halves were separate. By the mid-1970s he was running a portrait commission business, a magazine and a film operation, and The Philosophy of Andy Warhol is where he said the quiet part out loud: the deal-making was not a distraction from the work, it was the work.

Read in place, the line is also a joke at the expense of a particular audience. Warhol frames it as a reply to the counterculture’s reflex that money and work were somehow disreputable — which is why lifting the punchline out and printing it over a stock photo of a skyline gets the tone exactly backwards.
detailsBody: The Philosophy of Andy Warhol reads like Warhol talking because it largely is. Wikipedia’s account of the book describes it as ghostwritten by Pat Hackett and Bob Colacello, drawn from taped interviews Hackett recorded with Warhol for the book and from conversations Warhol had taped between himself, Colacello and Brigid Berlin.

That does not make the sentence less his — it is his voice, published under his name, in his lifetime — but it does explain why the line has the cadence of speech rather than of prose, and why so many people remember it as something Warhol said in an interview.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's sourced 1970s section attributes the full "business art" passage, ending "making money is art and working is art and good business is the best art", to The Philosophy of Andy Warhol: (From A to B and Back Again), 1975, p. 92.

The Philosophy of Andy Warhol (From A to B & Back Again) was published in 1975 by Harcourt Brace Jovanovich and was ghostwritten by Pat Hackett and Bob Colacello from taped interviews with Warhol and taped conversations involving Colacello and Brigid Berlin; the reception section reproduces John Raymond's 31 August 1975 Atlanta Journal-Constitution review quoting Warhol on "business art" and "Being good in business is the most fascinating kind of art."
The Internet Archive holds a 266-page scan of the 1975 Harcourt Brace Jovanovich edition of The philosophy of Andy Warhol: from A to B and back again, marked access-restricted (controlled lending).

Open Library's work record for The Philosophy of Andy Warhol (From A to B and Back Again) by Andy Warhol gives first publication 1975 and lists the 1975 and 1977 Harcourt Brace Jovanovich editions plus a 2006 Harcourt edition and a 2001 Italian edition.

The Art Story's Andy Warhol page reproduces the quotations "Business art is the step that comes after Art. I started as a commercial artist, and I want to finish as a business artist" and "Being good in business is the most fascinating kind of art ... Making money is art and working is art and good business is the best art", attributed to Warhol without a book citation.

The Andy Warhol Museum's biography page states Warhol was born Andrew Warhola on 6 August 1928 in Pittsburgh to immigrant parents, died in New York City on 22 February 1987, graduated from Carnegie Institute of Technology in 1949 with a BFA in Pictorial Design, and was a leading 1950s commercial illustrator for clients including Tiffany & Co., The New York Times, Columbia Records and NBC.
